Osimertinib is FDA approved for first-line treatment of NSCLC with an EGFR variant (e.g., EGFR exon 19 deletion).

answer: Targeted therapy plays a key role in EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). question: How does treatment differ between localized and metastatic non-small cell lung cancer?
answer: For localized (resectable) NSCLC, patients may be cured by surgery or surgery followed by chemotherapy. For metastatic (advanced) NSCLC, treatment aims at improved survival and palliation of symptoms using chemotherapy, targeted agents, and other supportive measures. In selected patients with solitary brain metastasis and no extracranial tumor, surgical excision with postoperative whole-brain radiation therapy, or stereotactic radiosurgery for unresectable lesions, can achieve prolonged disease-free survival.

question: When is chemotherapy used in non-small cell lung cancer?

question: What is the role of surgery in non-small cell lung cancer treatment?
answer: Surgery is the treatment of choice for patients with stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with lobectomy or segmental, wedge, or sleeve resection performed as appropriate; sublobar resection by anatomical segmentectomy or wedge resection is effective for clinical stage T1a, N0 NSCLC when intraoperative sampling of hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes is negative. For resectable stage IIIA NSCLC, if complete resection of tumor and lymph nodes is possible, patients may benefit from surgery followed by postoperative chemotherapy. Lung cancer resection combined with complete ipsilateral mediastinal lymph node dissection (CMLND) is not associated with improvement in survival compared with resection combined with systematic sampling of mediastinal lymph nodes in stage I, II, or IIIA NSCLC. The addition of surgery to chemoradiation therapy for stage IIIA NSCLC did not improve overall survival in a phase III trial but did improve progression-free survival. Surgical resection is also described as the primary treatment for early-stage lung cancer.

question: When is radiation therapy used for non-small cell lung cancer?
answer: Radiation therapy is used in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in several settings: as radiation therapy alone, it may benefit patients with locally advanced unresectable stage III NSCLC, and with traditional dose/fractionation schedules (1.8–2.0 Gy per fraction per day to 60–70 Gy over 6–7 weeks) it produces reproducible long-term survival benefit in 5%–10% of patients and significant palliation of symptoms. It is also an integral part of treatment for Pancoast tumors, and in some cases endobronchial laser therapy and/or brachytherapy has been used to alleviate proximal obstructing lesions. For tumors that invade the chest wall, radiation therapy is reserved for cases with unclear resection margins. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been studied in elderly patients with stage I–II NSCLC.

question: How is recurrent non-small cell lung cancer generally managed?
answer: Recurrent NSCLC is managed according to the site and extent of recurrence and the patient's performance status. For patients with a solitary brain metastasis after resection of a primary NSCLC lesion and no extracranial tumor, prolonged disease-free survival can be achieved with surgical excision of the brain metastasis plus postoperative whole-brain radiation therapy; unresectable brain metastases in this setting may be treated with stereotactic radiosurgery. Among patients who develop brain recurrence after resection and postoperative radiation therapy, those with good performance status and without progressive extracranial metastases may be offered reoperation or stereotactic radiation surgery; for most patients, additional radiation therapy can be considered, though its palliative benefit is limited. More generally, treatment options for progressive stage IV, relapsed, and recurrent NSCLC include second-line therapy, and patients with advanced metastatic disease may achieve improved survival and symptom palliation with chemotherapy, targeted agents, and other supportive measures.

answer: Maintenance therapy is described for patients with stable or responding disease after four cycles of platinum-based combination chemotherapy. question: What are common treatment strategies for small cell lung cancer?
answer: Common treatment strategies for small cell lung cancer (SCLC) include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, which have been shown to improve survival. Chemotherapy improves survival in both limited-stage (LD) and extensive-stage (ED) disease, though it is curative in only a few patients. The combination of platinum and etoposide is the most widely used standard chemotherapeutic regimen. For extensive-stage SCLC, treatment options include combination chemotherapy, commonly given as a two-drug combination of platinum and etoposide; cisplatin requires fluid hydration and has significant toxic effects, while carboplatin is active, dosed according to renal function, and associated with less nonhematological toxicity. Other regimens appear to produce similar survival outcomes but have been studied less extensively or are in less common use. Doses and schedules used in current programs yield overall response rates of 50% to 80% and complete response rates of 0% to 30% in ED SCLC. Intracranial metastases from small cell carcinoma may respond to chemotherapy. Localized forms of treatment, such as surgical resection or radiation therapy, rarely produce long-term survival because patients tend to develop distant metastases. For SCLC with liver metastases, immuno-chemotherapy is a pivotal therapeutic strategy for extensive-stage SCLC, though it fails to confer significant efficacy in liver metastases; other approaches include anti-angiogenic therapy, radiotherapy, microwave ablation (MWA)/radiofrequency ablation (RFA), trans-arterial chemoembolization (TACE), and systemic therapies with local interventions. In small cell carcinoma of the cervix, local therapy alone gives almost no chance of cure, and combination chemotherapy regimens such as vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide (VAC) or etoposide and cisplatin (EP) are used.

Late toxicities are uncommon and can be minimized with radiation delivery techniques and careful delineation of the target.

question: What factors influence prognosis and treatment planning in adult acute myeloid leukemia?

question: How is chronic lymphocytic leukemia generally managed?

question: How does biomarker testing influence treatment selection in non-small cell lung cancer?
answer: In advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), treatment decisions have become dependent on tissue and/or blood biomarkers. Comprehensive molecular profiling of DNA, RNA, and proteins can be performed to guide treatment. Liquid biopsy platforms detect circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and commonly cover mutations in genes such as EGFR, KRAS, and BRAF, as well as ALK rearrangements; plasma NGS platforms allow broader multi-gene testing. question: What is the role of surgery in non-small cell lung cancer treatment?
answer: Surgery is the treatment of choice for patients with stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); lobectomy or segmental, wedge, or sleeve resection may be performed as appropriate, with sublobar resection (anatomical segmentectomy or wedge resection) being effective for clinical stage T1a, N0 disease when intraoperative hilar and mediastinal lymph node sampling is negative. For resectable stage IIIA NSCLC, patients with occult N2 disease discovered at surgery may benefit from surgery followed by postoperative cisplatin combination chemotherapy if complete resection of tumor and lymph nodes is possible; however, the addition of surgery to chemoradiation therapy for stage IIIA NSCLC did not improve overall survival in a phase III trial, though it did improve progression-free survival. The optimal sequence of surgery and chemotherapy and the benefits and risks of postoperative radiation therapy in resectable NSCLC remain to be determined.

question: When is radiation therapy used for non-small cell lung cancer?
answer: Radiation therapy is used in several settings for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC): (1) Radiation therapy alone may benefit patients with locally advanced unresectable stage III NSCLC; with traditional dose and fractionation schedules (1.8–2.0 Gy per fraction per day to 60–70 Gy over 6–7 weeks), it produces reproducible long-term survival benefit in 5% to 10% of patients and significant palliation of symptoms. (2) Endobronchial laser therapy and/or brachytherapy has been used in some cases to alleviate proximal obstructing lesions. (3) Radiation therapy is an integral part of treatment for Pancoast tumors, though variations in dose, technique, and staging make its effectiveness difficult to determine. (4) For tumors that invade the chest wall, radiation therapy is reserved for cases with unclear resection margins (adjuvant chemotherapy is recommended). (5) Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) delivers curative-intent radiation to patients with early-stage NSCLC and inoperable thoracic lesions.

question: What factors influence first-line therapy selection in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer?
answer: Factors influencing first-line therapy selection in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer include comorbidity, performance status, histology, and molecular and immunologic features of the cancer. For patients without driver mutations, immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with or without chemotherapy is established as first-line treatment.

answer: Stage has a critical role in selecting therapy for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). question: What is the role of maintenance therapy in advanced non-small cell lung cancer?
answer: Maintenance therapy after first-line chemotherapy is used for patients with stable or responding disease after four cycles of platinum-based combination chemotherapy. However, the improvement in PFS is tempered by an increase in adverse events, including additional cytotoxic chemotherapy, and no consistent improvement in quality of life. For patients with stable disease or response to first-line therapy, evidence does not support continuing combination cytotoxic chemotherapy until disease progression or initiating a different chemotherapy before disease progression.

question: What are common treatment strategies for small cell lung cancer?
answer: Common treatment strategies for small cell lung cancer (SCLC) include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, which have been shown to improve survival. The combination of platinum and etoposide is the most widely used standard chemotherapeutic regimen for both limited-stage and extensive-stage disease. For extensive-stage SCLC, combination chemotherapy with a two-drug platinum and etoposide regimen is standard, with overall response rates of 50% to 80% and complete response rates of 0% to 30%. Cisplatin requires fluid hydration and has significant toxic effects, while carboplatin is dosed according to renal function and is associated with less nonhematological toxicity. More recently, anti-PD-L1 agents atezolizumab and durvalumab have been approved for first-line treatment in combination with chemotherapy for extensive-stage SCLC (immuno-chemotherapy). For SCLC with liver metastases, management beyond standard immuno-chemotherapy includes anti-angiogenic therapy, radiotherapy, microwave ablation/radiofrequency ablation, trans-arterial chemoembolization, and systemic therapies combined with local interventions.

question: What is the role of chemotherapy in small cell lung cancer?
answer: Chemotherapy has a central role in small cell lung cancer (SCLC). It improves survival in both limited-stage disease (LD) and extensive-stage disease (ED), although it is curative in only a few patients. Because SCLC tends to develop distant metastases, localized treatments such as surgery or radiation therapy rarely produce long-term survival, and incorporating chemotherapy into the treatment program prolongs survival, with at least a fourfold to fivefold improvement in median survival compared with no therapy. The combination of platinum and etoposide is the most widely used standard chemotherapeutic regimen. For limited-stage disease, combined-modality treatment with etoposide and cisplatin plus thoracic radiation therapy is the most widely used approach. In patients who have undergone surgery and are then diagnosed with SCLC, adjuvant chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy is generally given. No consistent survival benefit has resulted from platinum versus nonplatinum combinations, increased dose intensity or dose density, altered mode of administration, or maintenance chemotherapy.

Nanoparticle-based strategies, such as solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs), are being explored preclinically to improve targeted delivery and reduce adverse effects.

answer: Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is generally treated with chemotherapy, with the goal of achieving complete remission (CR) because partial remission offers no substantial survival benefit. question: What are common treatment strategies for small cell lung cancer?

Monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab and pertuzumab have proven highly beneficial, and additional HER2-directed strategies include bispecific antibodies (e.g., zanidatamab), antibody-drug conjugates (e.g., T-DM1, trastuzumab deruxtecan/T-DXd), and small-molecule inhibitors (e.g., lapatinib, neratinib, pyrotinib). These agents are used in metastatic disease, where they have revolutionized treatment and improved outcomes, and in early breast cancer, including neoadjuvant therapy with taxanes plus anti-HER2 therapies and adjuvant trastuzumab, for which 1 year of therapy is beneficial. Dual HER2 blockade and EGFR/HER2 dual-targeted drugs can help overcome resistance associated with HER2-targeted monotherapy. Resistance to anti-HER2 therapies can still develop, so personalized strategies based on tumor characteristics and treatment response are recommended.

question: What is the role of surgery in colon cancer treatment?
answer: Surgery is a primary treatment modality for colon cancer. Standard treatment for localized disease has been open surgical resection of the primary tumor and regional lymph nodes. Adjuvant radiation therapy has no current standard role following curative resection, although it may have a role for patients with residual disease.

question: How is adult acute myeloid leukemia generally treated?
answer: Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is generally treated with curative intent. Treatment should be sufficiently aggressive to achieve complete remission (CR), because partial remission offers no substantial survival benefit. Approximately 60% to 70% of adults with AML can be expected to attain CR after appropriate induction therapy. Consolidation therapy is always indicated when treatment is planned with curative intent; in a small randomized study, all patients who did not receive consolidation therapy relapsed after a short median CR duration. Nontransplant consolidation therapy using cytarabine-containing regimens has treatment-related death rates usually less than 10% to 20% and reported long-term disease-free survival rates from 20% to 50%; the optimal doses, schedules, and duration of consolidation chemotherapy have not been determined. Cytogenetic and molecular analyses provide the strongest prognostic information and predict outcome of both remission induction and consolidation therapy.

question: How is newly diagnosed adult acute myeloid leukemia managed?
answer: For newly diagnosed (previously untreated) adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML), treatment is selected based on disease phase and the patient's overall health status, with treatment intensity adjusted accordingly. The cornerstone of therapy is intensive chemotherapy, and treatment should be sufficiently aggressive to achieve complete remission (CR), because partial remission offers no substantial survival benefit. Approximately 60% to 70% of adults with AML attain CR after appropriate induction therapy, and more than 25% of adults with AML (about 45% of those attaining CR) can be expected to survive 3 or more years and may be cured. Successful treatment requires control of bone marrow and systemic disease, plus specific treatment of central nervous system (CNS) disease if present. Conventional cytogenetic analysis is mandatory in evaluation, and molecular diagnostics for recurrent somatic pathogenic variants (e.g., NPM1, FLT3, CEBPA, RUNX1) are routine for determining prognosis; cytogenetic and molecular analyses provide the strongest prognostic information, predicting outcome of both remission induction and consolidation therapy. Patients with unfavorable genetics or those who do not achieve remission may be candidates for bone marrow transplantation. Supportive care includes transfusions, antibiotics, and colony-stimulating factors; prior to therapy, patients should be well hydrated, and if WBC counts are high, allopurinol may be started to prevent hyperuricemia and renal insufficiency from tumor lysis syndrome. Myeloid sarcoma, even if apparently isolated, is a partial manifestation of systemic disease and should be treated with intensive chemotherapy.

question: What is the role of stem cell transplantation in adult acute myeloid leukemia?
answer: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) is used as consolidation therapy for adults with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in first complete remission (CR), with the goal of cure. In a donor-no donor comparison design, newly diagnosed AML patients who achieve CR and are medically eligible undergo HLA typing; if a matched sibling or matched unrelated donor is identified, the patient is allocated to the transplant arm, and analysis is by intention to treat. A meta-analysis of 18 prospective trials (adult patients aged 60 years and younger, enrolled 1982–2006) compared allogeneic transplant with autologous transplant or consolidation chemotherapy (most commonly high-dose cytarabine). Most physicians who treat leukemia agree that transplant should be offered to AML patients in first CR in the setting of adverse-risk features. Because HCT can cure more than 30% of patients who relapse after chemotherapy, some investigators have suggested that allogeneic bone marrow transplant can be reserved for early first relapse or second CR without compromising the number of patients ultimately cured. Clinical and cytogenetic information can define subsets of patients with better or worse prognoses based on favorable- and adverse-risk factors when using consolidation chemotherapy.

Measurable residual disease (MRD) in patients in complete remission is an important prognostic marker, with persistence of mutated NPM1 or FLT3-ITD before allogeneic transplant associated with increased relapse and death. Presence of myeloid sarcoma in otherwise good-risk t(8;21) AML may be associated with lower CR rate and decreased remission duration, and myeloid sarcoma should be treated with intensive chemotherapy.

question: How is chronic lymphocytic leukemia generally managed?
answer: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is generally managed conservatively and individualized based on the clinical behavior of the disease, because it is generally not curable, occurs in an older population, and often progresses slowly. Management ranges from observation with treatment of infectious, hemorrhagic, or immunological complications to a variety of therapeutic options given as single agents or combination therapy. In asymptomatic patients, treatment may be deferred until disease progression and symptoms occur; because progression rates vary and periods of stability or spontaneous regression can occur, frequent and careful observation is required. Even asymptomatic patients with del(17p) on FISH (or a TP53 pathogenic variant) may be followed with watchful waiting. With the introduction of B-cell receptor inhibitors and BCL2-targeted therapy, median survival has not been reached with over 10 years of follow-up.
